product.title: Korean 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Korean: romanization printed right above every hangeul syllable, short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Korean builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary, exercises, and an answer key. Includes a hangeul chart, the sound-change rules, a particle summary, both number systems, and a table of A1 verb forms. Written for English speakers — each unit targets one of the spots learners most often get wrong, from 은/는 vs 이/가 to choosing the wrong speech level.

cover_design.label: KOREAN
cover_design.ringkas: A self-study course in Korean for complete beginners — from reading hangeul in a single sitting to telling the story of last weekend.
cover_design.catatan: Romanization is printed above every syllable, with a word-for-word translation under every line of dialogue.

blocks.text: Many people come to Korean through an unusual door. They don't find it in a classroom but in TV dramas, songs, cooking channels and comment sections. That means most learners have already logged hundreds of hours of listening before writing a single letter — a head start that hardly any learner of German or Italian has.

That head start is real, but it's also deceptive. A trained ear makes people feel they're already halfway there, when what they've picked up is fragments: 오빠, 진짜, 괜찮아, 사랑해. All of them are **반말** — intimate speech, exactly what's most risky for a foreigner to use with someone they've just met. This module will ask you to set it aside for now and start with forms that are safe to use with anyone.

The good news: hangeul, the Korean alphabet, is no obstacle. It isn't a thousand-year inheritance like Chinese characters or Japanese kana but a **design** — created deliberately in the fifteenth century so that ordinary people could learn it in a matter of days. The consonant shapes mimic the mouth as it makes each sound. A motivated learner can usually read Korean signs after one sitting, and this module is built for exactly that: two pages up front for the letters, then straight into sentences.

The more honest news: what's hard about Korean isn't the alphabet but three things with no real counterpart in English. **First, particles** — small pieces that attach to the end of a noun to mark its role in the sentence. **Second, word order** that puts the verb at the very end, so a sentence only completes its meaning on the last word. **Third, speech levels** — the same sentence takes different shapes depending on who you're talking to, and picking the wrong one isn't a grammar error but a breach of manners, which is felt far more.

All three are set up in the early units and practiced again right up to the last. The twenty units cover the whole framework of A1 Korean: greeting and introducing yourself, pointing to things, the two number systems, talking about places and time, telling what happened yesterday, shopping and ordering food, saying what you want and can do, declining politely, asking for directions, and joining two sentences into one.

Each unit is one study session: twenty to thirty minutes. The dialogues are short and deliberately sound like real conversation, not example sentences. Under every line there's a word-for-word translation — Korean word order forced into English, often sounding odd, and that's exactly the point: it shows how Korean really organizes its thoughts before you smooth them into natural English.
Enjoy learning. 화이팅!

front.title: Contents
front.intro: This module works best in order — each unit reuses what the previous ones put in place.

blocks.text: This module follows the Assimil method: instead of memorizing a list of rules and then trying to build sentences, you absorb whole sentences first and let the rules follow. That's why the order in which you work through each unit matters.
Six steps for one unit

items: **Read the dialogue once, out loud, without looking at the meaning.** Romanization is printed above every syllable so your eyes don't have to jump down. Sound first, meaning later.
**Read it again with the translation lines.** The second line is natural English; the third (small italics) is the **literal** translation — word for word, following Korean order.
**Read the notes.** That's where the real substance of the module is. The notes explain why the sentence works the way it does, and almost always point out one mistake typical of learners.
**Read the grammar box**, then go back to the dialogue and find the examples. A rule you've just read sticks much better when you find the evidence in the sentences yourself.
**Do the exercises on paper, not in your head.** Writing hangeul by hand is the fastest way to lock in the letter shapes. The answer key is at the end of the unit — cover it first.
**The next day, reread yesterday's dialogue** before starting a new unit. Five minutes. This is what separates people who finish twenty units and remember from those who finish and forget.

blocks.text: How to read the romanization in this module

The romanization uses South Korea's official system (*Revised Romanization*) with one important adjustment: it shows **the sound that actually comes out**, not the spelling. That's why 감사합니다 is written *gamsahamnida* — not *gamsahabnida* — and 좋아요 is written *joayo*. The sound-change rules are explained two pages on.

blocks.title: A warning about romanization
items: The romanization in this module is **a temporary aid**, not a goal. It's there so you can get into sentences on day one, not so you depend on it in month three.
From unit 10 on, cover the romanization line with a piece of paper when you reread old dialogues. If you can still manage, you've graduated to hangeul — and that's exactly the target of an A1 module.

front.title: Hangeul: an alphabet designed, not inherited

blocks.text: Almost every writing system in the world grew slowly out of pictures. Hangeul didn't. It was **proclaimed** in 1446 by King Sejong together with a book explaining it, with the reason stated plainly on its first page: Chinese characters were too hard for ordinary people, so many had something to say but no way to write it down.

The result is an alphabet that can be explained in two pages. The basic consonants **imitate the shape of the speech organs** as the sound is made: ㄱ shows the back of the tongue bending up to the palate, ㄴ the tip of the tongue touching the upper gum, ㅁ a closed mouth, ㅅ a tooth, ㅇ an open throat. The other consonants are these basic shapes with extra strokes for stronger sounds: ㄱ→ㅋ, ㄴ→ㄷ→ㅌ, ㅁ→ㅂ→ㅍ.

The vowels are built from three symbols: a vertical line (human), a horizontal line (earth), and a dot, now written as a short stroke (heaven). ㅏ is a human with the sun on its east side; ㅗ is the earth with the sun above it. Adding one more stroke adds a *y* sound in front: ㅏ→ㅑ, ㅗ→ㅛ.
What you really need to understand: hangeul is written in syllables

This is the only part that differs from writing in the Latin alphabet. Korean letters aren't lined up one by one; they're **packed into square blocks**, one block per syllable. 한 is three letters, ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ, stacked into one block, not three letters in a row.

blocks.title: ㅇ has two jobs
items: **At the start of a syllable ㅇ is completely silent.** It's just a placeholder, because every hangeul block must begin with a consonant. 아 is read *a*, not *nga*.
**At the end of a syllable ㅇ sounds *ng*.** 강 = *gang*, 방 = *bang*. The same letter, two jobs, decided by its position in the block.
A classic beginner mistake: reading 이름 as *ngireum*. The correct reading is *ireum*.

blocks.text: The difference between these three kinds of consonant (plain – aspirated – tense) **doesn't exist in English**, and it's the hardest part of Korean pronunciation. Don't fight it now: it takes ears, not tables. What matters is knowing that the difference exists and changes the meaning of words.

blocks.title: The two vowel pairs most often mixed up
items: **ㅓ (eo) vs ㅗ (o).** For 어 the lips are relaxed and the jaw drops; for 오 the lips are rounded and pushed forward. 정 *jeong* ≠ 종 *jong*. Learners almost always say both as *o*.
**ㅡ (eu) vs ㅜ (u).** For ㅡ the lips are **not** rounded at all — pull them to the sides as if smiling faintly. 그 *geu* ≠ 구 *gu*.
**ㅐ and ㅔ are practically identical** in the speech of young Koreans. Don't waste time telling them apart; just learn how each word is spelled.

front.title: Sound rules you need to know

blocks.text: Korean is written one way and read another — not because the spelling is a mess, but because it deliberately keeps **the original form of each word** while the mouth adjusts. The four rules below explain almost all of the gap, and you've already met three of them in the first sentence of this module.
1. Linking (연음) — the final consonant jumps forward
When a syllable ends in a consonant and the next syllable starts with (silent) ㅇ, that consonant **moves over** to fill the empty slot.
This rule is why the romanization in this module sometimes seems not to "match" the letters. What's written is the sound.
2. Only seven final sounds
Any consonant can stand at the end of a syllable, but only seven sounds actually come out: **ㄱ ㄴ ㄷ ㄹ ㅁ ㅂ ㅇ**. The rest merge into one of them.

head: Final letter
Sounds like
Example
rows: ㅅ ㅆ ㅈ ㅊ ㅌ ㅎ
ㄱ ㄴ ㄹ ㅁ ㅂ ㅇ

blocks.text: These final sounds **are not released** — 밥 *bap* ends with the lips closing and stopping there, with no puff of air afterward, unlike an emphatic English *p* in "stop!".
3. Assimilation to nasal sounds
A hard final consonant that meets ㄴ or ㅁ softens into a nasal. This rule explains the most important word in the whole module.
That's why the polite ending *-습니다* is always written with ㅂ but always read *-seumnida*. Never read it *-seubnida*.
4. Tensing after a held sound
A plain consonant that comes right after a final ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ sound becomes tense (doubled), without this being written.

blocks.title: Don't memorize these rules now
items: The four rules above are placed up front so you **recognize them when you meet them**, not so you memorize them today. The romanization in each dialogue already applies them for you.
If the romanization ever seems to stray from the written letters, come back to this page. Nine times out of ten the answer is one of these four rules.

blocks.text: Particles are the backbone of Korean. They attach to the **end** of a noun and tell you that word's role in the sentence — a job English does with word order and prepositions. As long as the particles are right, Korean word order can be shuffled without changing the meaning; get a particle wrong and the sentence can mean the opposite.
Every particle below has already been used in the module. This page is for quick reference, not for memorizing in one sitting.

blocks.text: 은/는 vs 이/가 — a one-read summary

head: Use 은/는 when…
Use 이/가 when…
rows: Introducing or setting the topic of conversation
Answering "who/what" — picking one out of several
Mentioning something for the first time in a story
The sentence states something general about the topic
After 누구, 뭐, 어느 in a question

blocks.title: The three most common particle mistakes
items: **Using 에 for activities.** 식당**에** 먹어요 is wrong. An activity happens at a place → 식당**에서** 먹어요. 에 is only for *to* and *is at*.
**Double particles.** 저는도 is wrong — 도 **replaces** 은/는; it doesn't stack. The correct form is 저도.
**Dropping particles in writing.** In fast conversation Koreans often drop 은/는 and 을/를, but in writing and on the TOPIK they're required. Don't copy spoken habits until the full forms are automatic.

back.title: The two number systems and counters

blocks.text: Korean uses **two** sets of numbers that can't stand in for each other: native Korean numbers and Sino-Korean numbers borrowed from Chinese. Choosing the wrong one is the most common mistake foreign learners make in their first year, and it's instantly noticeable.
Which one to use when

head: Native Korean numbers
Sino-Korean numbers
rows: Counting things: 사과 세 개 (three apples)

blocks.title: Ten past seven, half past seven
items: **One time expression uses both systems at once.** 일곱 시 십 분 = ten past seven: **일곱**, a native number, for the hour, and **십**, a Sino-Korean number, for the minutes.
This isn't chaos — hours are counted as a *quantity* (native Korean), minutes are read as a *number* (Sino-Korean). Once you accept that, it never confuses you again.
Half = 반 *ban*. 일곱 시 반 = half past seven.

blocks.text: The order is always **noun + number + counter**: 커피 두 잔, not 두 잔 커피. That's the reverse of English ("two cups of coffee") and needs conscious practice until it's automatic.
Days
Time words
Months — Sino-Korean number + 월
Two months break the pattern: June should be 육월 but is written and read **유월**, and October should be 십월 but becomes **시월**. The reason is simply ease of pronunciation. Learn these two separately.

Dates always go from largest to smallest: **year – month – day**. 2026년 8월 23일 = August 23, 2026, read *icheon-isimnyungnyeon parwol isipsamil*. Year first, then month, then day — the reverse of the British day-month-year order.
Telling the time
The words you'll need most at A1, sorted alphabetically by English so you can look them up from the opposite direction to each unit's vocabulary list.

If you've reached this page after really working through all twenty units — not just skimming them — you're now at about **TOPIK I level 1**: roughly 400 words, the whole framework of basic Korean sentences, and the ability to get by in slow everyday conversation. You can introduce yourself, buy things, order food, ask for directions, tell the time, and say what you did yesterday.
That's far more than people imagine a "beginner level" to be, and far more than six months of watching dramas with subtitles can give you.
The next four steps, in order

items: **Drop the romanization right now.** Take units one to four, cover the romanized line with paper, and reread them out loud. The first five minutes will feel slow and painful; by day three it will feel normal. This is the one crutch you mustn't keep carrying.

**Push your vocabulary to 800 words before chasing new grammar.** At this point you get stuck not because you don't know the patterns but because you don't know the words. Ten words a day for two months is enough.

**Start listening without English subtitles.** Switch to Korean subtitles, not to no subtitles at all — that jump is too big. Variety shows and cooking vlogs are far friendlier to beginners than historical dramas.

**Find a real conversation partner.** Speech levels can't be fixed through two hundred hours of self-study; you need someone who corrects you the moment you accidentally use 반말 with someone older. This is where a teacher stops being a luxury.
